docs.title: FinGuard AI
docs.text:
Real-time financial fraud detection that explains every decision it makes.

FinGuard scores each transaction from 0 to 100 using three independent signals: fixed rules, a trained machine-learning model and an anomaly detector. It shows a fraud analyst exactly why a payment was flagged, and it learns from the analyst's verdicts.

Run it locally Read the design

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Traditional fraud systems check transactions against a fixed rulebook. That fails in three predictable ways.

Weakness Consequence Rules only catch patterns someone has already written down New fraud goes undetected until a rule is added by hand Every signal is weighed the same regardless of context Honest customers are blocked as often as fraudsters The system cannot say why it blocked a payment Analysts must reconstruct the evidence manually

docs.title: What FinGuard does
docs.text:
• Scores every payment from 0 to 100 and maps it to one of four actions: approve, verify, hold or block.
  • Combines three signals. A rule engine, an XGBoost classifier and an Isolation Forest run together, and a weighted aggregator produces one score.
  • Explains the result. Each score comes with a breakdown by signal and the model's own feature attributions (TreeSHAP).
  • Separates duties. Customers, fraud analysts, risk managers and administrators each see only what their role allows, enforced on the server.
  • Learns from decisions. Analyst verdicts become training labels. An administrator can retrain the model, and the new version goes live only if it passes a champion/challenger check.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Part State Scoring API, roles and audit log Built and tested (30 automated tests) Models trained on a public synthetic dataset Built, with stress tests Web console for all four roles Built Continuous learning with promotion gate Built Deployment In progress

Scope

This is an educational prototype. The dataset is synthetic, so the reported metrics describe that dataset and not real-world performance. See Machine learning for the limitations.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text: The API is served by FastAPI. When the backend is running, interactive documentation is at http://localhost:8000/docs.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Sign in with POST /auth/login to get a token, then send it on every other request.

POST /auth/login
{"username": "analyst", "password": "finguard-demo"}

{"token": "eyJ...", "role": "analyst", "name": "Neha Kapoor"}

Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
Rule Behavior Missing, expired, tampered or wrongly signed token 401 Valid token, role not allowed 403 Five wrong passwords for one username within a minute 429 Role Read from the database on every request, never from the client

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text: Method Path Allowed roles Purpose GET /health Anyone Check the server is running POST /auth/login Anyone Exchange a username and password for a token GET /auth/me Any signed-in user Return the current user and role GET /meta Any signed-in user Merchant categories and amount range for the forms POST /score Analyst, Risk Manager, Administrator Score a transaction without storing it POST /transactions Customer Make a payment: score it, store it, open a case if High or Critical GET /my-cases Customer The customer's own cases GET /cases Analyst, Risk Manager, Administrator Open cases, highest score first POST /decision Analyst Record Confirmed fraud, False positive or Escalated GET /audit Analyst, Risk Manager, Administrator Every decision with the role that made it GET /model Risk Manager, Administrator Label counts and retraining history POST /retrain Administrator Retrain and apply the champion/challenger check POST /demo/new-pattern Administrator Add simulated labelled records for a demo

docs.title: Scoring a transaction
docs.text:
Request fields use the dataset's column names.

POST /score

{
  "amount": 900,
  "transaction_hour": 3,
  "merchant_category": "Electronics",
  "foreign_transaction": true,
  "location_mismatch": true,
  "device_trust_score": 20,
  "velocity_last_24h": 6,
  "cardholder_age": 35
}

The response has the score, the tier, the recommended action, the contribution of each signal, and the model drivers. The numbers below are an example.

{
  "score": 90,
  "probability": 96,
  "tier": "Critical",
  "action": "Block and open an investigation case.",
  "parts": [{"label": "ML model", "points": 46.2}, {"label": "Rules", "points": 20.0}],
  "drivers": [{"feature": "Device trust", "impact": 34}, {"feature": "Amount", "impact": 22}]
}

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: FinGuard is a React web console in front of a FastAPI service. The service scores payments, stores cases and decisions in SQLite, and serves the trained models.

docs.title: How a payment is scored
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Customer payment] --> B["API: login token and role check"]
    B --> C[Feature extraction]
    C --> D[Rule engine]
    C --> E["XGBoost and Isolation Forest"]
    C --> F["Behavior, device and geography signals"]
    D --> G["Risk aggregator<br/>50 / 20 / 15 / 10 / 5"]
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H{Risk tier}
    H -->|Low| I[Approve]
    H -->|Medium| J[Verify with customer]
    H -->|High or Critical| K[Open case for an analyst]

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Layer What it is Where Web console React and Vite, one page for the public site and a role-based console src/frontend/ API FastAPI with JWT login and role checks on every route src/backend/main.py, auth.py Detection Features, rules, model inference, aggregator, explanations, retraining src/backend/detection/ Storage SQLite: users, cases, audit log, transactions, model versions src/backend/db.py Training Script that trains XGBoost and Isolation Forest and saves them src/ml/train.py

docs.title: Risk score
docs.text:
The final score is a weighted sum of five signals, each scaled from 0 to 100.

Signal Weight Source ML model 50% 80% XGBoost fraud probability and 20% Isolation Forest anomaly score Rules 20% Thresholds on amount, hour, foreign use, location, device trust and velocity Behavior 15% Transactions in the last 24 hours and night-time activity Device 10% Inverse of the device trust score Geography 5% Foreign transaction and billing/transaction location mismatch Score Tier Action 0 to 30 Low Approve automatically 31 to 60 Medium Verify with the customer and keep monitoring 61 to 80 High Hold the transaction and alert an analyst 81 to 100 Critical Block and open an investigation case

Illustrative weights

The weights are a design choice and have not been calibrated against live data. A production system would tune them.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Role Can do Customer Make payments and see the status of their own cases Fraud Analyst Review the case queue and record decisions. The only role that can decide Risk Manager Read the queue, use the score tool, view the audit log and model status Administrator Read the queue and audit log, view model status, retrain and manage models

The role is never taken from the browser. A signed token names the user, and the server looks the role up in the database on every request.

docs.title: Continuous learning
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Payment scored and stored] --> B[Analyst reviews case]
    B -->|Confirmed fraud or false positive| C[Record gets a label]
    C --> D[Administrator triggers retrain]
    D --> E[Challenger model trained]
    E --> F{"Better on new records,<br/>not much worse on old?"}
    F -->|Yes| G[Promoted, previous version archived]
    F -->|No| H[Live model kept]
    G --> A

Run these from the repository root.

python -m venv venv

docs.title: Dataset
docs.text:
The models are trained on a public credit-card fraud dataset of 10,000 synthetic transactions.

Property Value Rows 10,000 Fraud rows 151 (1.51%) Features used amount, transaction hour, merchant category, foreign transaction, location mismatch, device trust score, transactions in last 24 hours, cardholder age Target is_fraud

The identifier column is dropped and the merchant category is one-hot encoded. Because the data is synthetic, its labels follow a pattern a model can learn almost perfectly. The results below show that the pipeline works, not how it would perform on real bank data.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Model Type Role XGBoost Supervised Probability that a transaction is fraud Isolation Forest Unsupervised How unusual a transaction is, with no labels needed Rule engine Deterministic Fixed thresholds, also used as a baseline

The ML signal combines the two models, 80% XGBoost and 20% Isolation Forest.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Data is split 80/20 with stratification. The decision threshold is chosen from cross-validated predictions on the training part, never from the test part. The test set holds 30 fraud rows.

Method Precision Recall Rules only 0.28 1.00 XGBoost 1.00 1.00 Measure Value XGBoost PR-AUC (test) 1.00 XGBoost PR-AUC (5-fold cross-validation) 0.9975 ± 0.0035 Isolation Forest ROC-AUC, no labels used 0.95 Highest single-feature ROC-AUC (device trust) 0.83

The rules catch every fraud but also flag most honest transactions. The model keeps the recall and removes the false alarms. A score this high on clean synthetic data is an upper bound, not a promise, which is why the stress test below exists.

docs.title: Stress test
docs.text:
Each level is run with five random seeds and the mean PR-AUC is shown. At level 0 there is no noise.

Noise level Label noise Feature noise 0.0 1.000 1.000 0.1 0.997 0.645 0.2 0.988 0.418 0.3 0.955 0.276 0.5 0.829 0.133
  • Label noise hides a share of the training fraud labels and adds the same number of false alarms. The model holds up well, because the pattern in the data is strong.
  • Feature noise blurs the test transactions with noisy amounts, shifted hours and flipped flags. Scores fall quickly, so the clean-data result depends on exact inputs.
  • ROC-AUC under feature noise stays above 0.85 even at level 0.5, so the model still ranks risky transactions above safe ones. What it loses is precision at the top of the ranking.

docs.title: Explaining a decision
docs.text:
Every score returns two views.

  1. Signal breakdown. How many points each of the five weighted signals contributed.
  2. Model drivers. TreeSHAP values from XGBoost, shown as each feature's signed share of influence. A positive share pushes the score toward fraud. Merchant-category columns are merged into one driver.

docs.title: Learning from new data
docs.text:
The system folds analyst decisions back into the model.

  1. Every payment is stored with its features.
  2. When an analyst confirms fraud or marks a false positive, the stored record gets a label of 1 or 0. Escalated cases stay unlabelled.
  3. An administrator triggers retraining. XGBoost trains on the original data plus the new labels, weighted five times a normal row. Isolation Forest learns from every stored transaction, labelled or not.
  4. A champion/challenger check decides whether the new model replaces the live one. It must not lose more than 0.05 PR-AUC on the original holdout, and it must improve on a share of the new records that were held back from training.
  5. If it passes, it goes live and the previous model is archived. If not, the live model is kept. Either way the attempt is logged.

Result of one run on a simulated new fraud pattern:

Check Live model New model Original holdout, PR-AUC 1.000 0.980 Held-back new records, PR-AUC 0.790 1.000

An earlier, stricter check rejected this same model because it only compared against the original data. It would never have let the system learn anything new. Checking both sets fixed that.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The dataset is synthetic, so the metrics are not evidence of real-world accuracy.
  • The test set has only 30 fraud rows, so single results are noisy. Cross-validation is the more reliable figure.
  • Retraining is triggered by an administrator. It is not real-time online learning.
  • Only flagged cases are reviewed, so new labels lean toward suspicious transactions. The original data keeps the model anchored.
  • A wrong analyst verdict becomes a wrong label. The promotion check and archived versions limit the damage.

docs.title: Prototype
docs.text: The prototype is a working end-to-end system: customers pay, payments are scored, analysts review, and decisions feed back into the model.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text:
Start the backend and frontend as described in Installation, then follow one case through the whole system.

  1. Customer. Sign in as r.mehta, open Make a payment, and send a normal payment. It is approved. Then send a suspicious one: late hour, foreign transaction, location mismatch, low device trust. It is held or blocked and returns a case reference.
  2. Fraud Analyst. Sign in as analyst. The case is in the queue with its score, flags and the model's reasons. Confirm fraud. The stored payment now has a training label.
  3. Administrator. Sign in as admin, open Model, and see the labelled count rise. Add simulated records, then retrain. The page reports whether the new model was promoted and the before and after scores.
  4. Permissions. Sign in as risk. The case buttons are read-only. A customer cannot open the queue, the score tool or the model page.

docs.title: What is implemented
docs.text: Area Included Scoring Rules, XGBoost, Isolation Forest, weighted aggregator, four risk tiers Explainability Signal breakdown and TreeSHAP model drivers Security Password hashing, signed tokens, server-side roles, rate-limited login Workflow Case queue, analyst decisions, audit log Learning Stored payments, label capture, retraining with promotion check and model archive Quality 30 automated tests, stress test, rules-only baseline

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• The dataset is synthetic, so accuracy figures describe the dataset only.
  • Retraining is triggered by an administrator and is not continuous.
  • The login token is kept in browser session storage. A production system would use secure cookies and HTTPS.
  • There is no password reset or user-management screen. The four accounts are seeded.
  • SQLite replaces the proposed PostgreSQL and Redis, and there is no message queue.

Expect 30 passed. Two model tests are skipped until python src/ml/train.py has been run, and the end-to-end retraining test also needs the dataset in src/ml/data/.
